speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of Finance whether he would obtain from the Canadian Wheat Board a report on the extent of the deficit in the amount of grain moved out of Alberta to the west coast this season compared with last season and also whether he could ascertain from the Canadian Wheat Board the date by which this serious situation will be remedied, particularly in regard to the C.P.R. shipping points.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as was indicated yesterday, the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Agriculture and I met today with representatives of the C.P.R. to discuss this very question. The urgency of the situation at Vancouver is fully realized on all sides and the Canadian Pacific Railway representatives reiterated the assurance they had given me at the beginning of the year that they would fulfil their commitments under the contracts into which the Canadian Wheat Board had entered.

maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister whether he intends to follow the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture and have this matter investigated. There is a commitment from the C.P.R. but we are still on a one bushel quota. Does the minister intend to have this matter investigated? As the hon. member for Medicine Hat has indicated, this is a very serious question, particularly in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST
speechtext:
The seriousness of the situation is well understood by both the government and by the wheat board. The C.P.R. is not the only reason why the quotas are low in certain parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
46	COMMONS
Inquiries of the Ministry In order to fulfil the enormous contracts which have been entered into it was understood that the decision to move grain which was dry and in the most available positions at this season of the year would mean a great diversity of quotas. This has happened. It is not surprising. The C.P.R. fully understands, and before the end of the season they hope that the situation at its shipping points will be comparable to that in other parts of the west.

maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST
speechtext: A further supplementary question. The hon. gentleman has mentioned that the presence of certain dry and damp grains in the province of Alberta is the reason for the discrimination. Would he now explain to the house why the quota at all the C.N.R. points is seven bushels while on the C.P.R. it is only one or two bushels, as was stated by the Minister of Agriculture when he was in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST
speechtext: The hon. member for Bow River has distorted my statement. I did not say what he now says I did. I said that because of the urgency of the shipping situation there was bound to be a considerable disparity in quotas at this season of the year, and this problem has been complicated by the damp grain situation. All concerned, including the C.N.R., the C.P.R. and the Canadian Wheat Board, will do their best before July 31 to improve these quotas as quickly as possible.

maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST

maintopic: REPORTED DELAYS IN GRAIN MOVEMENT TO WEST COAST
speechtext:
I will allow the Minister of Agriculture to speak for himself, of course. Mr. Speaker, in rising to deal with the motion now before the house I wish at once to extend my very sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer) and the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) on the manner in which they placed before the house, in their respective maiden speeches,

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker their views and ideals. I will not say I agreed with all of their conclusions but that is to be expected.
It is always a matter of great interest to anyone who has been in the house over the years to see young men and women come into this chamber, because new members and returning old members give lifeblood to this house which strengthens the mission of parliament. I do not wish to single out any one member but I am sure the house will not raise any objection if I refer to the fact that there is one member here who, by reason of the association of her late husband and her late father with this house, deserves special mention. I refer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis).
That hon. member's late husband, Angus Maclnnis, was one of those members of this house who spoke fearlessly with the authority of idealism. He gave fine representation in the best traditions of this house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

Her father was here but a short while after I came as a new member. Illness struck him but he returned to this chamber on one or two occasions thereafter. I heard him speak. He was a man whose life was given in devotion to the things in which he believed. He was a socialist; he advocated socialism and was not afraid to stand for the things in which he believed.
I recall watching that hon. member from the gallery of this house at the time of the outbreak of war. That was before I became a member. He rose and spoke. What he said was not acceptable to a great majority of the members of the house but they listened with an attitude that is characteristic of parliament.
This same thing happened on another occasion when the late Hon. P. J. Cardin rose in the house during the dark days of the war. What he said did not have complete approval, but the fact that he was listened to with intense feeling on the part of all reflects something of the meaning of this institution. We must preserve those things that are worthwhile.
At this time, sir, I must, in something less than a purely formal sense, extend my congratulations to you. What I said the other day remains unrevised and unrepented. It requires no change of wording. As Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition my congratulations are extended to you in ample measure. We have seen you in action and we
January 20, 1966

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker appreciate the dignity, capacity and ability that you have displayed in the discharge of your high office in a matter of a few hours.
Now, sir, I am going to speak for a moment about parliament before I start to deal in some detail with the Speech from the Throne. And lest anyone thinks I am going to continue these commendatory words, I immediately give warning that I am not. But this parliament, and parliament in general, is something that we must do our part to preserve.
The idea is getting around today that parliament needs to be changed. The efficiency experts speak of parliament as though it were a kind of directors' meeting where efficiency is the objective. Parliament is no such thing. Parliament is a place where freedom is maintained. Parliament is not a place where we administer; parliament is not a place whose value depends on the number of statutes that are passed. Parliament is a place where we assure that the administration shall be carried out honestly and effectively.
Parliament is not a place to be operated, as I said a moment ago, like a business. The opposition has a responsibility in parliament and that responsibility is to do its part to examine carefully, to criticize strongly where necessary and to stand when the government endeavours to bring about measures that in the opinion of the opposition, conscientiously arrived at, are not for the benefit of the people.
There is a philosophy growing up that amendments have something sinister about them. I know my hon. friends opposite do not belong to that school because when they were in opposition amendments, votes of non-confidence, were prolifically produced. The record speaks for itself. Suddenly these people opposite have become paragons of parliamentary perfection. We are living in a new era. Even my friends of the New Democratic party who speak today of phony amendments seem to forget their contribution to parliament while we were in office.

I do not mind interruptions. Finally, on the 20th of January the first motion was made by the Liberal party. It was moved by the present right hon. Prime Minister and seconded by Mr. St. Laurent. I
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker need not go into it. It was one in which they said that in view of the desirability of having a government pledged to implement Liberal policies His Excellency's advisers should, in the opinion of this house, submit their resignation forthwith.
In those days amendments such as these were proper. I never criticize the making of amendments, because they are necessary to parliament. Suddenly, under the new philosophy, you must not deal with those things. You have got to bring about a new parliamentary system. My hon. friends of the N.D.P. recognize this fact. The leader of the socialist party in the United Kingdom does not raise that objection with a government that hangs by a thread. Regularly there have been motions of non-confidence and amendments.
Now, sir, I am not for the moment going into the period between 1958 and 1962.

All through that period the hon. gentlemen who now sit on the treasury benches moved amendments on every occasion. I have them here. There was nothing at that time sinister or detrimental to parliament in that connection.
Now I come to 1962. In 1962 when parliament met, a motion was moved immediately by hon. gentlemen who sit opposite. They continued to raise these motions on several occasions. They were finally successful on a subamendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). They were together then. The subamendment referred to the government's failure to pursue any financial policies based on Social Credit principles designed to establish a balanced economy and so on. Indeed, in the fall of 1962 on one such amendment the Liberal party voted for debt free money.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Those were the days before the Liberal party was able to bring into the house three wise men. I say nothing more about that at the moment.
Those were days when on every occasion questions were raised by way of amendment. We never took any objection to that because that is parliament. Are you going to have an opposition stand for something, say that they believe in this and this and this, go through an election campaign standing for certain principles that are just as valid today as they were then, and then, when they come into the
January 20, 1966

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker House of Commons, not bring up these things? They say we will be holding up the institution if we do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is the same old gang.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Sir, it is necessary that we study parliamentary principles, if the greatness of our tradition is to be preserved. Remove that and all you would do would be to get up in the house and speak and, having spoken, not vote. That is what they are trying to get the people of Canada to believe today, that there is something very wrong in members of a party standing up in parliament and calling on the government to do something that they ought to do. I have never found that the greatness of parliament could be upheld by those who endeavour to turn it into a body for talk but with no vote.
Now, sir, I come to the Speech from the Throne. I do not have to spend much time on that. It has all the earmarks of "Kentish" origin because the words of Mr. Kent in the last Speech from the Throne with a few additions, have been repeated with almost photostatic exactness.
You will remember that we were told that all that was necessary to bring about bold and imaginative government was to return those who today sit opposite. What has been produced is a puerile, pusillanimous piece of repetitive propaganda. Oh, they go marching by. There is reference to the Canadian economy. Mention is made of the preservation and the strengthening of Canadian identity and unity. The question of dominion-provincial relations is touched on in a rather careful way.
A few months ago in the previous Speech from the Throne they had a formula to amend the constitution and bring it back to Canada. Nine provinces said yes. Where is that now? It is put in these words:
It remains the objective of my Ministers to provide that the Constitution of Canada may be amended in Canada.
It is a delightful document. There is a reference to the fact that the Canadian people can be well served by their political institutions only if each element in our federal system is able to act effectively within its constitutional sphere. I am going to come back to the reorganization of the cabinet in a moment. The ministers do not seem to know yet who is who or who is responsible for what when questions are asked.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
When the Prime Minister issued his press release he said that bankruptcy, he thought,


would come under the purview of the President of the Privy Council I thought that an unusual place. After all, bankruptcy was one matter over which his Minister of Justice had authority. The year 1965 saw $500 million worth of bankruptcies. It was the greatest open season for wrongdoing that Canada has ever seen. The act is going to be amended but never is. Then the Throne Speech refers to economic development, and about that I may say something in a moment.
With regard to education there is an addition here. We took a strong stand on the subject of education. We said that the time had come when action must be widespread and massive while preserving the constitutional and exclusive authority of the provinces over education. Anything the government brings in in this connection which will preserve and maintain this constitutional safeguard will not be one of the matters that we will oppose.
As I go along through the speech I see our old friend the Canada Development Corporation has come to life again. In 1963 this matter was vital. In 1964 it did not appear in the Speech from the Throne at all. In 1965 it was resuscitated. Again it is brought in, and I wonder what will happen to it. Will it actually be introduced and proceeded with?
Then the question of capital punishment is mentioned. I think this question should be dealt with at once. I have had some experience in the courts and I have strong feelings on this subject. When we came into office we took the stand that anyone convicted of murder, who was given a recommendation to mercy by the jury, ought not to be executed, for such a division of opinion among the jury would indicate that there had been serious reason for the determination made by that jury. While the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) was minister of justice we brought about reform in this connection by dividing murder into two groups, capital and non-capital murder. I know what this means and I can understand the feelings of anyone who, as prime minister, has to sign the document. But we took the stand that where there was cold-blooded, premeditated murder the law either meant something or it did not and we carried it out.
What has happened recently in this connection? There should be no exception to this rule. But we have a government which has made the administration of capital punishment something beyond what could ever have been contemplated. Naturally I do not know
January 20, 1966

the facts of the various cases, but there are two or three cases in respect of which, so long as the law is as it is, I find the reprieves that have been granted difficult to understand. I hope that this uncertainty will be removed one way or the other and at once. I join with the Prime Minister in giving approval of and support to a free vote in the House of Commons, for we cannot go on with a law on the statute books which is partially carried out, indeed often derogated from.
So far as other sections of the Speech are concerned I will make some passing references, but I should like to say this. What we have in this Speech from the Throne is a caricature of what is needed in this country today. The Speech seems to have been the result of the right and the left trying to get together, the representatives of the great interests and the representatives of no interest trying to come to something which would be acceptable to all.
All of us know the circumstances surrounding the election. The Prime Minister said that he could not carry on without a majority. There are many quotations in this regard and they can be placed on the record in due course. He could not carry on and his various Ministers said the same. There they were, hamstrung, their hands tied. In one breath they said they were being interfered with. In the next breath they said to the people that they had the finest government there ever was. They told them to look at the wonderful record of legislation which the government had brought before parliament.
The essence, Mr. Speaker, of the election being called, in complete derogation of an implied undertaking on the part of the Prime Minister given in June last, was based on the excuse that they needed a majority, that they wanted support in all parts of Canada. There are now three provinces in which they have no representation. The government could not carry on unless they had representation across the country. This was the excuse.
I do not want to use a lot of words, Mr. Speaker, to describe this government and I want to remain strictly within the parliamentary tradition. The greatest parliamentarian of them all was Churchill. He got up on one occasion, I am not sure of the year, while he was leader of the opposition, looked over at the Attlee government and said:	"Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me to say so-I hope you will not call me to order-this is a lousy government". Then he went on to say: "That expression is not used in a contemptuous
The Address-Mr. DiefenbaJcer way; it is simply a narrative of a situation". That is what Churchill said on one occasion. All through the years that he spoke formidably in the house there was none of this new philosophy that the House of Commons is to be a kind of glorified kindergarten. Just read the debates, Mr. Speaker, which took place between Aneuran Bevan and Churchill, one man who, above all others, Churchill did not always decide to cross swords with.
This is a floundering government, Mr. Speaker. It has bumbled, bungled, boxed and bewildered' itself. In case the Prime Minister thinks I am using too strong language, I might recall his words before he developed a new philosophy in September, 1963.

I had that experience. I have never told it. But I have read some biographers of the late President Kennedy, biographers who, I hope, come closer to the truth than some in Canada do. The United States took a strong stand against our selling wheat to Communist China. Today the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) spoke of the tremendous sales which had been made.

Sir, in the international field we are endeavouring at all times to be in agreement. I do not intend to deal with the international situation today except to say that at this time, when one of the great Commonwealth Prime Ministers retires from office-I refer to Sir Robert Menzies-the Commonwealth faces one of the most serious challenges to its continuing existence in its short but glorious history. I will at all times join in hoping that whoever the Prime Minister of Canada may be he will carry out to the fullest extent possible the ameliorating processes that will bring about the kind of settlement which was achieved between Pakistan and India only a few days ago. It is a matter of serious consequence, as the effort is made to meet Communism in all parts of the world, that we within the Commonwealth could not bring about a settlement and that it took the U.S.S.R. to achieve something which we had not been able to obtain.
In the national field I say deliberately that this is a government which has whittled away the basic principles of Confederation. It has bent to demands. It has virtually brought about a position in this country whereby provinces may become, if not sovereign states, associated states. I am glad to see that there are now some in the Liberal party who are standing against that. I think of the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau), already honoured as Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister. Read what he has to say about this idea of special status for any one province or associate states. He takes the strongest possible objection. It is of interest that when we took that stand we were pictured as being anti-Quebec. What was heresy when we stood for it is now approaching orthodoxy within the Liberal party.

Indeed, they have fallen short of what the United States has been able to achieve in the same period. They have fallen short of the gain made in productivity in Canada from 1950 to 1955, the previous period of high economic growth. The Economic Council of Canada placed the issue squarely before the Canadian people, when at page 33 of its review it said:
The most important current problem is to achieve and maintain adequate productivity growth. This is the key to economic growth and to rising living standards for Canadians.

The fact is that our economy is not yet operating at full potential. Our ability to raise living standards, to wage war on poverty and to contribute to the needs of the world's underdeveloped areas depends on our being able to increase Canada's productivity.

Some of my colleagues will be dealing with aspects of these problems. I want to deal, as briefly as I can, with four important factors in increasing productivity, namely education, manpower training, health and social security.
May I deal first with education as a major factor in promoting increased productivity. The Economic Council in its review finds that although price levels in Canada and the

United States are roughly equal, the level of income in Canada is about 25 per cent lower than in the United States. This income gap is difficult to understand when one recalls that over the past 50 years Canada has had certain advantages over the United States. Firs* we have had a larger shift of manpower from low-paid agriculture to higher levels of income in other sectors of the economy. Second, we have had a higher level of capital investment per employed worker. Third, we have had a more rapid rate of increase in population.
The Economic Council maintains that the explanation for the lower level of Canadian income per employed person lies in the educational gap and in the difference in quality of technological skills between the two countries. The Bladen report pointed out that less than one Canadian in ten between the ages of 18 and 24 is attending a university or college, whereas in the United States the ratio is much closer to one in three. The Economic Council points out that the educational gap between Canada and the United States appears to have widened, particularly at the secondary school level during the inter-war years and at the university level during the post-war years. In 1960, 45 per cent of the male labour force in the United States had four years high school education, as compared to only 24 per cent in Canada. In the same year in the United States 11.1 per cent of the male labour force had completed university; in Canada the figure was 5.6 per cent.
We have come to the place, Mr. Speaker, where educational opportunity is not only an individual right but a social necessity if we are to enjoy increased productivity and hence higher standards of living. During the past half century United States productivity has remained ahead of Canada's because the United States has chosen to invest a greater proportion of its resources in education. The time has come for Canada to allocate vast sums of money for academic and technical education at all levels, and particularly for upgrading the educational qualifications of those who are employed in jobs that have been, or are likely to be, eliminated by automation and technological change.
The Speech from the Throne makes reference to scholarships and bursaries, and this afternoon the Prime Minister announced an increase in grants to universities of an average of $5 per capita. I am sure that this will be welcomed in all parts of Canada and particularly in university circles.

However, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that we will not close this educational gap unless the government is prepared to do two things: first, provide universities and technical institutes with sufficient additional revenue so that they can eliminate entirely tuition fees; second, provide capital and construction grants so that the facilities can be increased and the number of teachers required trained to meet the student explosion which will certainly take place within the next five or ten years.
Scholarships and bursaries will help students meet living expenses. I think the government must move in the direction of the elimination of student fees, so that education is free and available to every person capable of making use of it, right from grade one up to as high in the educational and technical field as a student's ability will take him or her. I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that this investment will be more than repaid by the contribution which these young people will make to the Canada of the future. As a matter of fact, when one realizes that in 1960 the average income of a person who had completed high school was $2,000 a year more than a person who had only finished public school, and that a university graduate's income was on the average $3,700 a year higher than those who had completed high school, one can see that over their working lifetime these students will more than pay back in income tax alone the money which has been invested in their education by the people of Canada.
The second factor in productivity is manpower training. Economic growth depends on technical skill and the adaptability of our labour force. Last year the Economic Council pointed out the need for a manpower policy. The government tried to bluff this off as being an unwarranted criticism, but I am very glad to say that they have taken the criticism to heart.
The council pointed out that we needed three things. We needed first a proper administrative set-up, one department with all the agencies contributing to manpower needs under one minister. I am glad that the Prime Minister has decided to take that step; and the new minister, who I think has some excellent qualifications for the task, will have at his disposal all the ingredients necessary to produce a real manpower program, provided he gets from his colleagues the necessary funds to put such a program into effect.
The second thing which is required is a vast training and retraining program, not

Mr. Speaker, on July 19 and 20 last a federal-provincial conference was held to discuss medicare. At that time the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) laid down four excellent principles. The first was that at this stage medicare was to apply to physicians services, both general practitioner and specialist.
Second, the program was to have universal coverage. In his excellent speech, which I will not take the time to read extensively, the Prime Minister rejected the principle of "need theory"; he said he rejected it because it set up an undesirable distinction according to income level. The Prime Minister said no extension of private plans would meet all the needs. He said this plan should be universal on the same basis as hospital insurance coverage.
The third principle was that the plan should be administered by the provincial governments-that they must take full responsibility. He said it was necessarily a replacement of existing plans of other types.
The fourth principle was transferability. The Prime Minister pointed out that, like hospital insurance, medicare must be available to Canadians as they move from province to province and from place to place.
All of us were pleased by this statement from the Prime Minister, which was fully in accord with the recommendations of the Hall Commission. Mr. Speaker, I find it both sad and painful that Conservative members should be the first to repudiate the words of their leader who, but a few hours ago, spoke as the strongest defender of the traditions of this house.
Now, it has always been the tradition to recognize first the party leaders, that is, to give them the floor first during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I feel that this tradition, so strongly upheld this afternoon by the leader of the Conservative party, ought to be respected and that Conservative members should follow the words of their leader concerning the respect of tradition and allow party leaders to have the floor first, as it has been the custom since 1917, that is since there have been several parties in this house. Then, our democratic regime will be respected. I beg you, therefore, to recognize another party leader in the person of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette).
